name: Eastern Rome: A Thousand Years of Constantinople
description: The Roman Empire did not end in 476. In the east it lasted another thousand years, from Constantine's new city to the Ottoman guns of 1453.

checkpoints.name: Constantine's new city
checkpoints.note: Constantine the Great ended the persecution of Christians with the Edict of Milan, supported the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and founded a new capital on the Bosphorus in 330, the city later called Istanbul.

checkpoints.name: The age of Justinian
checkpoints.note: After the empire split, the eastern half became the Byzantine Empire. The Walls of Constantinople protected the capital, while the west fell in 476. Justinian I and his general Belisarius won back lands, Hagia Sophia was built, and from 541 the plague of Justinian struck the empire.

checkpoints.name: Survival and fire
checkpoints.note: After Justinian the empire fought to survive against Persians, Arabs and others. Byzantine ships used Greek fire against attackers, and ties with Kievan Rus brought Orthodox Christianity to the Slavic lands.

checkpoints.name: Turks and crusaders
checkpoints.note: The defeat at Manzikert in 1071 cost the empire much of Anatolia. The Council of Clermont launched the First Crusade, and in 1204 the Fourth Crusade attacked and sacked Constantinople itself.

checkpoints.name: The last centuries
checkpoints.note: The Byzantines retook their capital in 1261 but never regained their strength. The Ottoman Empire grew, Mehmed II captured the city in 1453, and the sultans built Topkapi Palace and the Sultan Ahmed Mosque.
